title: Beyond RSV: why the bronchiolitis burden in infants will not simply disappear.

analysis.scope_and_question: We argue, however, that these successes should not be mistaken for the resolution of severe bronchiolitis as a clinical and public health problem.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The supplied evidence does not clearly state the review method, databases, eligibility process, or evidence base.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: We contend that bronchiolitis should be understood as a syndrome reflecting the infant airway's stereotyped response to viral injury, rather than a disease defined by a single pathogen.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Second, although current evidence does not support viral replacement, the possibility that other respiratory viruses could expand into the ecological niche vacated by suppressed RSV transmission warrants close monitoring, alongside the theoretical, fitness-limited risk of nirsevimab-resistant RSV escape variants.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: We call for sustained broad spectrum viral surveillance to ensure that success against RSV translates into a durable reduction of the overall bronchiolitis burden, rather than its replacement by other pathogens.

analysis.summary_en: We argue, however, that these successes should not be mistaken for the resolution of severe bronchiolitis as a clinical and public health problem. The supplied evidence does not clearly state the review method, databases, eligibility process, or evidence base. We contend that bronchiolitis should be understood as a syndrome reflecting the infant airway's stereotyped response to viral injury, rather than a disease defined by a single pathogen. Second, although current evidence does not support viral replacement, the possibility that other respiratory viruses could expand into the ecological niche vacated by suppressed RSV transmission warrants close monitoring, alongside the theoretical, fitness-limited risk of nirsevimab-resistant RSV escape variants. We call for sustained broad spectrum viral surveillance to ensure that success against RSV translates into a durable reduction of the overall bronchiolitis burden, rather than its replacement by other pathogens.

title: Enhanced respiratory syncytial virus surveillance of young children admitted to the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network, 2019-2023.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to comprehensively describe the clinical characteristics, management and outcomes of children with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease admitted to the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network, determine the full burden of severe disease and identify population-specific risk factors for intensive care unit (ICU) admission.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a multi-centre, retrospective cohort study conducted over 5 years at two tertiary paediatric hospitals in metropolitan New South Wales, Australia, involving 4414 children aged <2 years hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed RSV, of whom 11.3% were admitted to ICU.
analysis.methods: The study was conducted at two tertiary paediatric hospitals in metropolitan New South Wales, Australia, before implementation of government-funded immunisation programs against RSV in children. The main outcome measures were characteristics and incidence rate of RSV hospitalisations and ICU admissions among children aged <2 years. Factors associated with higher odds of ICU admission were identified using multivariate logistic regression.
analysis.main_results: Over a 5-year period, 4414 children were hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed RSV, of whom 11.3% (499/4414) were admitted to ICU. The median age was younger in the ICU cohort (n = 499) compared with the non-ICU sample (n = 1000; 3.3 vs 7.1 months, P < 0.0001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating that RSV immunisation programs are expected to substantially reduce the burden of hospitalisation among Australian children in their first year of life. They also identified that Indigenous children, those born prematurely or with cardiac disease are at greatest risk of severe disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of targeted preventative programs for Indigenous children, those born prematurely and children with cardiac disease, as well as guide the implementation of RSV immunisation programs in Australia.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was conducted before the implementation of government-funded immunisation programs, which may limit its generalisability. The evidence is strong, with a high confidence assessment based on the comprehensive data collection and statistical analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted a multi-centre, retrospective cohort analysis of 4414 children aged <2 years hospitalised with laboratory-confirmed respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) at two tertiary paediatric hospitals in New South Wales, Australia, over 5 years. It found that 11.3% of these children were admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU), with younger age, prematurity, Indigenous identity, and cardiac disease being significant risk factors. The results highlight the need for targeted preventative programs and suggest that RSV immunisation programs could substantially reduce hospitalisation rates among young children. The study's findings are robust, with high confidence, but its limitations include the pre-implementation context of immunisation programs, which may affect generalisability.

analysis.scope_and_question: We developed and validated a tool to identify structural, informational, emotional, and social barriers.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A cross-sectional study based on a survey of mothers who were eligible to receive the RSV vaccine.

title: Rise of Lower Respiratory Tract Infections Other than Respiratory Syncytial Virus in the Emergency Room: Results from the Season (2024/25) of the RISE Study.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Acute respiratory infections (ARI) are a major cause of pediatric emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This prospective surveillance study quantified ARI-related ED visits, described pathogen-specific epidemiology, and assessed attendance and hospitalization rates as well as the distribution of lower versus upper respiratory tract infections (LRTI/URTI) in children younger than 60 months in two pediatric EDs in Berlin between November 1, 2024 and May 31, 2025.
analysis.methods: Respiratory pathogens were identified using nasopharyngeal swab samples tested by multiplex real-time RT-PCR (QIAstat-Dx® Respiratory Panel Plus).
analysis.main_results: Hospitalization due to LRTI predominated among children with RSV (24/26, 92.3%) and RV infections (20/28, 71.4%), whereas FLU infections were less frequently observed (7/13, 53.9%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Furthermore, younger age, a history of pneumonia, a history of bronchiolitis, and the absence of breastfeeding were associated with hospitalization.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings may impact surveillance strategies, clinical management, and future public health strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: In contrast to the previous season, in which RSV was associated with the highest attendance and hospitalization rate, we observed a high burden of RV infections in the 2024/2025 season.

analysis.summary_en: Acute respiratory infections (ARI) are a major cause of pediatric emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations. This prospective surveillance study quantified ARI-related ED visits, described pathogen-specific epidemiology, and assessed attendance and hospitalization rates as well as the distribution of lower versus upper respiratory tract infections (LRTI/URTI) in children younger than 60 months in two pediatric EDs in Berlin between November 1, 2024 and May 31, 2025. Respiratory pathogens were identified using nasopharyngeal swab samples tested by multiplex real-time RT-PCR (QIAstat-Dx® Respiratory Panel Plus). Hospitalization due to LRTI predominated among children with RSV (24/26, 92.3%) and RV infections (20/28, 71.4%), whereas FLU infections were less frequently observed (7/13, 53.9%). Furthermore, younger age, a history of pneumonia, a history of bronchiolitis, and the absence of breastfeeding were associated with hospitalization. These findings may impact surveillance strategies, clinical management, and future public health strategies. In contrast to the previous season, in which RSV was associated with the highest attendance and hospitalization rate, we observed a high burden of RV infections in the 2024/2025 season.

title: Respiratory syncytial virus in adults aged ≥ 50 years in the Netherlands: a database and time-series modelling analysis (2013-2020).

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a significant yet historically understudied contributor to acute respiratory infection (ARI) in older adults.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective cohort study (1 July 2013 to 29 February 2020) utilised routinely collected primary and secondary care data from the PHARMO Data Network to examine ARI-associated hospital admissions in patients aged ≥ 50 years.
analysis.methods: The number and annual rate of RSV- and influenza-associated ARI and lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) hospital admissions by age and risk group were estimated using a Quasi-Poisson regression model.
analysis.main_results: There were 97,279 ARI admissions in 63,420 patients. Estimated RSV-associated ARI hospital admission rates ranged from 0.70/1,000 person-years (PY) to 1.92/1,000 PY in adults aged ≥ 50 and ≥ 75, respectively.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study provides novel estimates of RSV-associated hospital admissions in adults aged ≥ 50 years, highlighting the substantial burden of RSV in this population.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the need for targeted RSV prevention strategies, particularly in high-risk individuals, to reduce the hospitalisation burden associated with RSV.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on routinely collected data and does not account for potential underreporting, which may affect the accuracy of the estimated RSV admissions.

analysis.summary_en: This study quantifies the hospitalisation burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in adults aged ≥ 50 years in the Netherlands using time-series modelling. It reports that there were 97,279 acute respiratory infection (ARI) admissions in 63,420 patients during 2013-2020. RSV-associated ARI admission rates ranged from 0.70 to 1.92 per 1,000 person-years, with higher rates observed in older adults and high-risk individuals. The study highlights the need for RSV prevention strategies, particularly in high-risk groups, to mitigate the substantial hospitalisation burden. However, the reliance on routinely collected data may introduce underreporting bias, limiting the strength of the evidence.

title: Under pressure: lessons learnt from rapid implementation of the respiratory syncytial virus maternal vaccine and infant nirsevimab in Sydney, Australia.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to share lessons from the rapid implementation of RSV prevention products and present data on immunisation uptake for mothers and babies in two maternity hospitals. The research was needed to address the challenge of integrating new RSV prevention strategies into routine clinical practice.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the rollout of the RSV maternal vaccine and the injectable monoclonal antibody nirsevimab in two maternity hospitals within the Sydney Local Health District. The study period spanned from February to September 2025, focusing on immunisation uptake among mothers and eligible newborns.
analysis.methods: Deidentified summary data from electronic medical records were analysed descriptively as counts and proportions. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research was used to evaluate the rollout process and identify factors influencing immunisation uptake.
analysis.main_results: RSV vaccination coverage in women giving birth in the two hospitals increased from 4% in the first month of rollout to 70-74% from June to September 2025. As antenatal coverage improved, the number of live born babies requiring nirsevimab decreased. Among eligible newborns, 36% of families declined nirsevimab, with reasons for refusal not recorded. Documentation of RSV immunisation status improved as the rollout progressed.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as evidence that coordinated engagement with multidisciplinary leaders and clinicians is critical for successful program rollout. The study highlights the importance of clear messaging and systemic safeguards in implementing multiple immunisation products for distinct groups.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of future RSV prevention programs by demonstrating the effectiveness of strategies such as clinician education and integration of immunisation into medical record workflows. They also provide insights into improving uptake and reducing refusal rates for RSV vaccines and monoclonal antibodies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on deidentified summary data and the absence of recorded reasons for refusal. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the descriptive nature of the analysis and the lack of detailed statistical or causal interpretations.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the rollout of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention products, including the maternal vaccine and the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab, in two maternity hospitals in Sydney, Australia. It reports that RSV vaccination coverage among mothers improved significantly from 4% in February 2025 to 70-74% by September 2025. As coverage increased, fewer newborns required nirsevimab. However, 36% of eligible families declined the antibody, with no recorded reasons. The study highlights the importance of multidisciplinary engagement and clear messaging in program implementation. It also notes that integrating immunisation into medical record workflows can support program adoption. The findings suggest that while the rollout was successful, the lack of detailed refusal data and the descriptive nature of the analysis limit the strength of the evidence. These insights can inform future RSV prevention strategies and improve immunisation uptake.

title: Secondary Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis after Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation in the Setting of an Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection: A Case Report.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Secondary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (SPAP) is rare and often results in poor outcomes; therefore, it is crucial to diagnose and treat it appropriately.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A 23-year-old man who received allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) 18 months before presentation was diagnosed with SPAP after allo-HSCT in the setting of an RSV infection.

title: Maternal Vaccination vs Nirsevimab Use and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection Among Full-Term Infants

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the relative effectiveness of maternal vaccination with RSVpreF versus infant nirsevimab in preventing RSV infection and hospitalization among full-term infants born in the 2023 to 2025 RSV seasons. Since 2023, infants can be protected from RSV through maternal vaccination or infant monoclonal antibody treatment.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective cohort study included full-term infants born at Kaiser Permanente Northern California from December 3, 2023, to March 30, 2024, or September 29, 2024, to March 15, 2025. Infants were matched based on birth week, sex, and maternal factors, with optimal full matching (up to 1:5) for RSVpreF vs nirsevimab and up to 1:10 for unprotected infants.
analysis.methods: The study used PCR-confirmed RSV infection and hospitalization as primary outcomes. Exposures were maternal RSVpreF at 32 to 36 weeks' gestation or infant nirsevimab through age 7 days. The main outcome measures were restricted mean time lost for infection and hospitalization in infants aged 8 to 180 days or through RSV season end (April 30 in both seasons).
analysis.main_results: Of 15,124 matched infants, 146 (0.97%) had RSV infection (106 in the RSVpreF group and 40 in the nirsevimab group) and 12 (0.08%) were hospitalized (7 in the RSVpreF group and 5 in the nirsevimab group). The rPE of RSVpreF vs nirsevimab was -5.3% (95% CI, -44.8% to 23.4%) against infection and 61.5% (95% CI, -10.8% to 86.7%) against hospitalization. Compared with no protection, RSVpreF had a 69.3% (95% CI, 59.9% to 76.6%) reduction in infections and 86.4% (95% CI, 66.4% to 94.5%) in hospitalizations; nirsevimab had a 65.2% (95% CI, 51.0% to 75.4%) and 73.8% (95% CI, 33.4% to 89.7%) reduction, respectively.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found no statistically significant difference between maternal RSVpreF and infant nirsevimab in RSV infection or hospitalization. Both products were associated with fewer infections and hospitalizations compared to no protection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This study supports current US guidelines for either maternal RSVpreF or infant nirsevimab to protect all infants from RSV, indicating that both methods are effective in reducing RSV infection and hospitalization rates.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and the potential for unmeasured confounders. The sample size was adequate for the primary analysis, but the confidence intervals for the rPE estimates are wide, indicating some uncertainty in the results.

analysis.summary_en: This study compared the effectiveness of maternal RSVpreF vaccination and infant nirsevimab in preventing RSV infection and hospitalization among full-term infants. No statistically significant difference was found between the two methods, but both were effective in reducing infections and hospitalizations compared to no protection.

title: Epidemiology and seasonality of respiratory syncytial virus among hospitalized pediatric patients with lower respiratory tract infections in Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia (2017–2024)

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the seasonality and exogenous factors influencing RSV cases among hospitalized children under 12 years in Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia, addressing the need to understand RSV's distinct seasonal patterns in tropical settings.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed weekly laboratory-confirmed RSV-positive cases among hospitalized pediatric patients with acute lower respiratory tract infections across 417 continuous WHO epidemiological weeks from 2017 to 2024, focusing on Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia.
analysis.methods: RSV dynamics were analyzed using decomposition and autocorrelation functions, and relationships with co-circulating viruses, meteorological variables, and holidays were assessed via cross-correlation and ARIMAX modeling.
analysis.main_results: A total of 6,545 (14.29%) samples were RSV-positive from 45,817 tested. Historical peaks were disrupted during 2020–2023 but re-established in 2024. The ARIMAX (2,0,4) (1,0,0) 52 model indicated that RSV dynamics were primarily driven by internal autoregressive patterns. Major public holidays showed a significant dual effect, with an immediate decrease followed by a surge in reported cases. Influenza activity was a significant predictor with a one-week lag.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the pandemic temporarily shifted RSV seasonality, which has since normalized. The associations with holiday periods and influenza activity indicate that behavioral factors and viral interference may influence RSV circulation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings emphasize the need for dynamic surveillance to optimize the timing of future RSV immunizations in Malaysia, highlighting the importance of understanding RSV's behavior in tropical settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's findings are limited by the reliance on historical data and the potential for confounding factors. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and the lack of randomized controlled trials.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed RSV cases among hospitalized children in Negeri Sembilan, Malaysia, from 2017 to 2024. It found that RSV seasonality was disrupted during the pandemic but has since normalized. Behavioral factors and viral interference were identified as influencing RSV circulation, emphasizing the need for dynamic surveillance.

title: Age-Related Differences in the Clinical Presentation of Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection in Hospitalized Children: A Three-Year Retrospective Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate age-related differences in clinical presentation and respiratory severity among children hospitalized with RSV infection, addressing the need to understand how age influences disease severity and clinical phenotype in infants and young children, given the highest risk of severe disease during early infancy.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted on 241 children aged 0–24 months hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed RSV infection between January 2022 and December 2024, across four age groups (0–3, 4–6, 7–12, and 13–24 months).
analysis.methods: Clinical manifestations were compared across age groups using multivariable logistic regression, adjusting for sex, prematurity, viral co-infection, and feeding type. The Holm procedure was applied to account for multiple comparisons.
analysis.main_results: Fever increased significantly with age, from 48.8% among children aged 0–3 months to 81.7% among those aged 13–24 months (p < 0.001). Each additional month of age was associated with higher odds of fever (aOR 1.090, 95% CI 1.045–1.137; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and lower odds of thoracoabdominal asynchrony (aOR 0.951, 95% CI 0.917–0.986; Holm-adjusted p = 0.044). Infants aged 0–3 months required oxygen more frequently than older children (46.5% vs. 25.3%) and had significantly higher adjusted odds of oxygen requirement (aOR 2.54, 95% CI 1.26–5.0; p = 0.009).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights age-specific clinical assessment and the vulnerability of infants during the earliest months of life, with younger infants exhibiting more prominent signs of respiratory distress despite a lower frequency of fever, and a particularly high likelihood of requiring supplemental oxygen.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings can inform surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for RSV infection, emphasizing the importance of age-specific clinical assessment and reinforcing the vulnerability of infants during the earliest months of life.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design, potential for selection bias, and the need for larger sample sizes to confirm findings. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated age-related differences in clinical presentation and respiratory severity among children hospitalized with RSV infection, finding that younger infants exhibit more prominent signs of respiratory distress despite a lower frequency of fever, and have a higher likelihood of requiring supplemental oxygen.

analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: It also discusses the role of immunity gaps, disrupted routine immunization, altered healthcare-seeking behavior, co-detection, and regional variation in India.

This narrative review summarizes pre-pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic respiratory pathogen patterns with emphasis on pediatric infections, global observations, and Indian data. Non-pharmaceutical interventions, including masking, school closure, distancing, improved hand hygiene, and reduced travel, were associated with a fall in several common respiratory viruses, particularly influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), while rhinovirus/enterovirus continued to circulate in many settings. Strengthening respiratory virus surveillance, improving access to multiplex diagnostics in sentinel centers, restoring routine immunization, and integrating influenza, RSV, and COVID-19 prevention strategies into pediatric public health planning are essential in the post-COVID period.

title: Co-Assembly of Ribavirin and TMC353121 Nanoparticles for Enhanced Inhibition of Respiratory Syncytial Virus-Induced Pneumonia as an Alternative Therapy

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore an alternative therapy for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection by investigating the feasibility of formulating ribavirin and TMC353121 into an RBA-TMC self-assembled nanoparticle (RTSN) and assessing its antiviral activity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the formulation of RBA and TMC into RTSN and assessed its antiviral activity through in vitro and in vivo experiments, including a mouse model of RSV-induced pneumonia.
analysis.methods: The methods included the formulation of ribavirin and TMC353121 into self-assembled nanoparticles, testing their antiviral activity through in vitro assays, and evaluating their efficacy in a mouse model of RSV-induced pneumonia.
analysis.main_results: The results showed that RBA and TMC formed RTSN through hydrogen bonding and π-π stacking interactions. RTSN exhibited antiviral efficacy with a selectivity index of 43.8 and an effective concentration (EC50) of 10.9 μM.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as demonstrating the potential of RTSN as an innovative treatment strategy for RSV, leveraging self-assembly technology to enhance antiviral activity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that RTSN could offer a new therapeutic approach for RSV, potentially improving antiviral efficacy and biosafety in treating RSV-induced pneumonia.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its use of a mouse model, which may not fully represent human RSV infection. The evidence is moderate due to the lack of clinical trials and long-term safety data.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the use of ribavirin and TMC353121 self-assembled nanoparticles (RTSN) as an alternative therapy for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. The research aimed to assess the feasibility of this formulation and its antiviral activity. Results showed that RBA and TMC formed RTSN through hydrogen bonding and π-π stacking interactions, with antiviral efficacy demonstrated by a selectivity index of 43.8 and an effective concentration (EC50) of 10.9 μM. The authors interpreted these findings as an innovative strategy for RSV treatment, leveraging self-assembly technology. The study's significance lies in its potential to enhance therapeutic options for RSV, particularly in treating RSV-induced pneumonia. However, the study is limited by its reliance on a mouse model, which may not fully reflect human conditions, and the evidence is considered moderate due to the absence of clinical trials and long-term safety data.

title: Temporal changes in pediatric respiratory syncytial virus and adenovirus positivity across COVID-19-related periods: A six-year retrospective cohort study

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate how the positivity rates of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and adenovirus changed over time among children during three distinct periods related to the COVID-19 pandemic, addressing the need to understand the impact of public health measures on these viral infections.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted across three periods: pre-pandemic (January 2018–February 2020), restrictive pandemic (March 2020–May 2021), and post-restriction (June 2021–June 2023). It included 8,253 children aged 0–18 years who underwent concurrent RSV and adenovirus antigen testing for suspected acute respiratory infection.
analysis.methods: Unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) were calculated from period-specific counts using the pre-pandemic period as reference. Positivity proportions were compared by period, with the pre-pandemic period serving as the baseline for analysis.
analysis.main_results: RSV was detected in 266 children (3.2%) and adenovirus in 612 (7.4%). RSV positivity was 1.5% (55/3,785) pre-pandemic, 1.2% (13/1,055) during restrictions, and 5.8% (198/3,413) post-restriction. Adenovirus positivity was 8.8%, 10.2%, and 5.0%, respectively, with corresponding ORs of 1.18 (95% CI 0.94–1.48) and 0.54 (95% CI 0.45–0.66) relative to the pre-pandemic period.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that RSV and adenovirus positivity followed different temporal patterns, with RSV positivity increasing significantly post-restriction compared to the pre-pandemic period, while adenovirus positivity showed a decrease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that changes in public health measures and healthcare-seeking behavior may have influenced RSV positivity rates, which could inform future surveillance and intervention strategies for pediatric respiratory infections.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on unadjusted odds ratios and potential confounding factors such as seasonality and testing practices. The evidence is moderate as it is based on a single-center retrospective analysis without controlling for these variables.

analysis.summary_en: This six-year retrospective cohort study examined temporal changes in respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and adenovirus positivity among children during three distinct periods related to the COVID-19 pandemic. The study included 8,253 children tested for suspected acute respiratory infection between January 2018 and June 2023. RSV positivity was 1.5% pre-pandemic, 1.2% during restrictions, and 5.8% post-restriction, with higher odds post-restriction. Adenovirus positivity decreased from 8.8% to 5.0% during the same periods. The authors concluded that these changes may reflect shifts in public health measures, testing practices, and healthcare-seeking behavior, rather than direct causal effects. The study provides insights into the impact of pandemic-related interventions on viral positivity rates but is limited by its unadjusted analysis and potential confounding factors, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

title: Recommendations for the Prevention of Respiratory Syncytial Virus Disease in Infants and Children: Technical Report

analysis.research_question_and_background: This report addresses the need for updated recommendations on preventing respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease in infants and children, focusing on immunization strategies during the 2026–2027 RSV season. The rationale for these recommendations is grounded in the current understanding of RSV epidemiology and disease burden.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a technical report that synthesizes existing evidence on RSV immunization effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness in pediatric populations. It includes recommendations for infants younger than 8 months and high-risk infants and children aged 8 through 19 months.
analysis.methods: The report compiles and evaluates current evidence on RSV epidemiology, disease burden, immunization effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness. It also provides an overview of available RSV immunization products and their formulations.
analysis.main_results: The report outlines the rationale for recommending immunization of all infants younger than 8 months born during or entering their first RSV season, unless the infant has documented protection from vaccination of the pregnant parent; and infants and children 8 through 19 months of age who are at high risk of severe RSV disease and entering their second RSV season.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the findings as supporting the expansion of high-risk groups for second season RSV immunization. The novelty lies in the updated recommendations for immunization based on the latest evidence.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform public health strategies for RSV immunization, particularly in identifying high-risk groups and optimizing vaccine administration schedules for infants and children.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on a synthesis of current literature, and the report does not include new data. The strength of the evidence is moderate, as it relies on existing studies rather than original research.

analysis.summary_en: This technical report provides updated recommendations for the prevention of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease in infants and children during the 2026–2027 RSV season. It outlines the rationale for immunizing all infants younger than 8 months and high-risk infants and children aged 8 through 19 months. The report synthesizes current evidence on RSV epidemiology, disease burden, immunization effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness. It also provides an overview of available RSV immunization products and formulations. The findings support the expansion of high-risk groups for second season immunization and can inform public health strategies. The evidence is based on existing literature, and the strength is moderate due to the reliance on synthesized data rather than original research.

title: Using HVR2-G in molecular epidemiology surveillance of HRSV: a supplement for the application of WGS

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the applicability of the HVR2-G sequencing window for lineage classification and integrate previous HVR2-G genotypes with the new WGS-defined lineage nomenclature. Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) is a major pathogen causing acute lower respiratory tract infections in infants, young children and older adults.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted using whole-genome sequence (WGS) data from GenBank and lineage nomenclature data from Nextstrain. The HVR2-G region was extracted from these sequences to assess its utility in lineage classification.
analysis.methods: The HVR2-G region was extracted from WGS sequences from GenBank and the lineage nomenclature data were downloaded from Nextstrain. Phylogenetic and nucleotide pairwise distance (p-distance) analyses of HVR2-G sequences were conducted using IQ-TREE 2.3.6 and MEGA11.0, respectively.
analysis.main_results: Phylogenetic analyses revealed that the primary lineages defined by WGS-defined lineage nomenclature could be classified using the HVR2-G region with a bootstrap over 70%; the nested lineages could not be distinguished. Nineteen and 37 previous HVR2-G genotypes of HRSVA and B were reduced to 4 (A.1, A.2, A.3 and A.D) and 5 (B.1, B.2, B.3, B.4 and B.D) lineages with P-distance thresholds greater than 0.102 and 0.0591, respectively.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study confirmed that the HVR2-G sequencing window provides reliable assignment of major HRSV lineages and enables integration with historical surveillance datasets. This approach has the potential to serve as a complement to the application of WGS for molecular virological surveillance of HRSV in China and globally, especially in resource-limited areas.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that HVR2-G sequencing can be used to enhance molecular epidemiology surveillance of HRSV, particularly in areas where WGS may not be feasible. This integration allows for the use of historical data in conjunction with modern sequencing techniques.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study does not address potential limitations in the generalizability of the HVR2-G sequencing window to other regions or populations. The evidence is moderate as it is based on analysis of existing sequence data rather than new experimental findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the applicability of the HVR2-G sequencing window for lineage classification of human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) and its integration with the new WGS-defined lineage nomenclature. The research highlights that the HVR2-G region can reliably classify major HRSV lineages with a bootstrap over 70%, but nested lineages remain indistinguishable. Previous HVR2-G genotypes of HRSVA and B were reduced to fewer lineages using P-distance thresholds. The study suggests that HVR2-G sequencing can complement WGS in molecular virological surveillance, especially in resource-limited settings. However, the evidence is moderate as it relies on existing sequence data rather than new experimental findings, and the generalizability of the results to other populations is not addressed.

title: Impact of Universal Nirsevimab Immunoprophylaxis on Bronchiolitis Hospitalizations and Disease Severity in Neonates: A Real-World Single-Centre Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the impact of universal nirsevimab immunoprophylaxis on bronchiolitis hospitalizations and disease severity in neonates, addressing the need to assess the effectiveness of this prophylaxis in reducing RSV-related hospitalizations and severity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective, observational study was conducted at a tertiary pediatric center in Rome, Italy, comparing four consecutive RSV seasons: pre-universal prophylaxis (2022–2024) with post-universal prophylaxis (2024–2026).
analysis.methods: The study included term and preterm infants ≤30 days and under term-corrected age hospitalized for acute bronchiolitis, with RSV status confirmed by viral testing within 72 hours of admission.
analysis.main_results: Total bronchiolitis admissions dropped by 52% (256 to 122), with RSV-positive cases decreasing from 66.8% to 43.4% (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.52–0.81; p < 0.001). Monthly peak RSV admissions fell progressively, and ICU rates dropped from 18.4% to 4.1% (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.09–0.55; p < 0.001). Among RSV-positive neonates, respiratory support requirements and ICU admissions also decreased significantly.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Universal nirsevimab prophylaxis was associated with marked reductions in neonatal bronchiolitis hospitalizations, RSV positivity, respiratory support needs, and ICU admissions, highlighting the effectiveness of early, high-coverage implementation prior to seasonal RSV peaks.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that universal nirsevimab prophylaxis can significantly reduce the burden of RSV-related bronchiolitis in neonates, potentially leading to improved clinical outcomes and reduced hospitalizations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its single-center design, which may affect generalizability. However, the high coverage and consistent results across two seasons support the robustness of the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the impact of universal nirsevimab immunoprophylaxis on bronchiolitis hospitalizations and disease severity in neonates. It found significant reductions in RSV-related hospitalizations, respiratory support needs, and ICU admissions, supporting the effectiveness of early, high-coverage prophylaxis.

title: Hospital-based surveillance of vaccine-preventable diseases in children: a retrospective study in a Dutch tertiary hospital (2024-2025).

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of using routinely collected hospital data for in-hospital surveillance of pediatric vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs), addressing the need to inform public health strategies and strengthen national immunization programs.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at a tertiary hospital in the Netherlands from July 2024 to June 2025, focusing on children <18 years old with laboratory-confirmed infections caused by pathogens with available licensed vaccines, regardless of their inclusion in the national immunization program.
analysis.methods: Feasibility was assessed based on case ascertainment, completeness of key variables, and availability of vaccination information, requiring integration of multiple data sources.
analysis.main_results: The study included 99 children (103 VPD episodes; median age 0.6 years), with 60% (n = 59) requiring pediatric intensive care. Most hospitalizations were caused by respiratory infections, particularly RSV (n = 52) and influenza (n = 27).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Retrospective hospital-based surveillance of pediatric VPDs is feasible and provides key information to guide efforts to optimize the national immunization program, complementing existing surveillance data in the Netherlands.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: By capturing disease severity and vaccine preventability, the study highlights the importance of integrating hospital data for surveillance, which can inform public health strategies and improve immunization programs.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the need for data integration from multiple sources and the fact that 9% of VPD episodes occurred in fully vaccinated children, suggesting potential gaps in vaccine coverage or effectiveness.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the feasibility of using hospital data for in-hospital surveillance of pediatric vaccine-preventable diseases, demonstrating its potential to inform public health strategies and improve immunization programs.

title: Neutrophils in Respiratory Viral Infection: Immunopathology and Therapeutic Strategies.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on the role of neutrophils in respiratory viral infections, particularly Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), with an emphasis on their immunopathological functions and therapeutic targeting potential.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a comprehensive summary of current knowledge on neutrophil biology and their roles in respiratory viral infections, including RSV, Influenza A virus (IAV), and Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). It includes preclinical and clinical studies on therapeutic approaches targeting neutrophils.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Neutrophils are critical in maintaining the mucosal barrier in the respiratory tract and are involved in both protective and pathogenic roles during infection. Their dysregulation is linked to disease severity and lung injury, making them a potential therapeutic target.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: There is ongoing debate about the dual roles of neutrophils in respiratory viral infections, with some evidence suggesting they contribute to inflammation and tissue damage beyond their antimicrobial functions. The review highlights the need for more research to clarify these mechanisms and develop targeted therapies.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Future research should focus on understanding the precise mechanisms by which neutrophils contribute to both host defense and pathological outcomes in RSV infections. Therapeutic strategies should aim to modulate neutrophil-driven inflammation without compromising their protective functions.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the immunopathological roles of neutrophils in respiratory viral infections, with a focus on Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV). It highlights the dual functions of neutrophils in both protecting the host and contributing to inflammation and tissue damage. The review emphasizes the need for targeted therapeutic strategies that balance their protective and pathogenic effects. It also discusses the importance of further research to clarify the mechanisms underlying neutrophil dysregulation in RSV infections and to develop effective interventions.

title: Comprehensive Performance Verification of the Mindray MN2880 System in Detecting Respiratory Virus Nucleic Acids.

analysis.research_question_and_background: To verify the clinical performance of the Mindray MN2880 system for simultaneous detection of SARS‐CoV‐2, influenza A virus (IAV), influenza B virus (IBV), and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) nucleic acids.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Comprehensive evaluation of the Mindray MN2880 multiplex respiratory virus assay across seven critical performance parameters: clinical concordance, limit of detection (LoD), repeatability, precision, cross‐reactivity/interference resistance, daily QC, and contamination control.
analysis.methods: Evaluation according to CNAS‐GL039:2019 and CNAS‐GL037:2019 requirements, including detection of SARS‐CoV‐2, IAV, IBV, and RSV nucleic acids with high diagnostic concordance, clinically verified limits of detection, and robust interference resistance.
analysis.main_results: High diagnostic concordance with reference method, clinically verified limits of detection (LoD: SARS‐CoV‐2 at 100 copies/mL, IAV/IBV/RSV at 200 copies/mL), 100% precision, and no observed cross‐reactivity.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The MN2880 system satisfies key analytical benchmarks required for diagnostic use in respiratory virus multiplex testing, with performance verified against CNAS‐GL039:2019 and CNAS‐GL037:2019 standards.

title: Antiviral Drug Development against RNA Viruses: Progress, Clinical Translation and Persistent Challenges

analysis.scope_and_question: This critical narrative review examines how viral biology, pharmacological exposure, disease timing, trial design, resistance and health-system access jointly determine whether an antiviral candidate becomes a clinically useful intervention.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: Peer-reviewed mechanistic studies, randomised trials, methodological papers and authoritative institutional evidence published from 2000 to 13 August 2026 were critically synthesised, with earlier foundational findings considered where necessary.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Contrasting remdesivir outcomes across disease stages, context-dependent results for oral coronavirus antivirals, a promising but geographically limited paediatric respiratory syncytial virus trial, and dengue human-challenge studies illustrate why positive virological or early clinical findings require precise interpretation.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The central conclusion is that antiviral innovation is most effective when molecular specificity, clinically relevant timing and equitable implementation are developed as a connected evidence pathway.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Priorities include pharmacologically credible discovery platforms, earlier diagnosis and treatment, adaptive trials with prespecified patient-important endpoints, resistance-informed combinations, outbreak-ready trial infrastructure and affordability planned before licensing.

analysis.summary_en: This critical narrative review examines how viral biology, pharmacological exposure, disease timing, trial design, resistance and health-system access jointly determine whether an antiviral candidate becomes a clinically useful intervention. Peer-reviewed mechanistic studies, randomised trials, methodological papers and authoritative institutional evidence published from 2000 to 13 August 2026 were critically synthesised, with earlier foundational findings considered where necessary. Contrasting remdesivir outcomes across disease stages, context-dependent results for oral coronavirus antivirals, a promising but geographically limited paediatric respiratory syncytial virus trial, and dengue human-challenge studies illustrate why positive virological or early clinical findings require precise interpretation. The central conclusion is that antiviral innovation is most effective when molecular specificity, clinically relevant timing and equitable implementation are developed as a connected evidence pathway. Priorities include pharmacologically credible discovery platforms, earlier diagnosis and treatment, adaptive trials with prespecified patient-important endpoints, resistance-informed combinations, outbreak-ready trial infrastructure and affordability planned before licensing.

title: Nasal Mucosal Immunity is Associated with Protection against RSV Illness in Infants

analysis.research_question_and_background: Despite advances in respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) immunoprophylaxis, RSV remains a leading cause of severe respiratory illness in infants.
analysis.study_design_and_population: We analyzed mucosal and serologic anti-RSV antibodies and assessed for factors impacting titer magnitude and durability.
analysis.methods: Specimens from 285 infants/young children and 39 mothers were analyzed.
analysis.main_results: Mucosal anti-RSV antibody levels were lower in infants presenting with RSV infection compared to age-matched controls both in infants experiencing their first viral season (p = 0.0011) and older children (p < 0.0001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These results suggest that RSV immunization strategies optimizing durable mucosal immunity may protect infants from RSV-related respiratory illness.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Higher levels of mucosal antibodies were seen in infants whose mothers received maternal pre-F vaccination, with IgG against RSV fusion protein tightly correlating between infant serum and nasal compartments (p < 0.0001).
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: This deterministic extraction is based on abstract only. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

analysis.summary_en: Despite advances in respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) immunoprophylaxis, RSV remains a leading cause of severe respiratory illness in infants. We analyzed mucosal and serologic anti-RSV antibodies and assessed for factors impacting titer magnitude and durability. Specimens from 285 infants/young children and 39 mothers were analyzed. Mucosal anti-RSV antibody levels were lower in infants presenting with RSV infection compared to age-matched controls both in infants experiencing their first viral season (p = 0.0011) and older children (p < 0.0001). These results suggest that RSV immunization strategies optimizing durable mucosal immunity may protect infants from RSV-related respiratory illness. Higher levels of mucosal antibodies were seen in infants whose mothers received maternal pre-F vaccination, with IgG against RSV fusion protein tightly correlating between infant serum and nasal compartments (p < 0.0001). This deterministic extraction is based on abstract only. The source does not explicitly report enough limitations for an independent appraisal, so confidence is low.

title: Data-driven forecasting of Flu, RSV, and COVID-19 related outcomes in the United States and Canada via Hankel dynamic mode decomposition.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the potential of data-driven dynamical modeling, specifically Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), for forecasting infectious disease outcomes, addressing the challenge posed by season-to-season variability and limited dynamical history.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study conducted a retrospective analysis of the 2024-2025 influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and COVID-19 seasons in the United States and Canada, comparing forecasts generated using Hankel-DMD against those submitted to the CDC's FluSight Forecast Hub and the University of Guelph's AI4CastingHub.
analysis.methods: Hankel-DMD was used to generate weekly forecasts, which were submitted to the FluSight Forecast Hub and AI4CastingHub for evaluation. The method was benchmarked against other models that submitted forecasts for the same seasons.
analysis.main_results: Hankel-DMD provided high-quality forecasts at the beginning and end of the season but significantly overestimated the peak during the middle of the season. This overestimation led to worse than baseline performance on the FluSight Forecast Hub.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that while Hankel-DMD is a promising method for forecasting infectious diseases, its performance during the season peak requires further refinement. The study highlights the potential of this method as well as its current limitations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results indicate that Hankel-DMD could be a valuable tool for forecasting respiratory syncytial virus and other infectious diseases, aiding in public health planning and resource allocation, particularly in regions with limited expertise.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's retrospective nature and the limited number of models used for comparison may affect the generalizability of the findings. The evidence is moderate, as the performance was evaluated across the entire season, and the method's effectiveness during the peak remains uncertain.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the effectiveness of Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) in forecasting respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and other infectious disease outcomes in the United States and Canada. The research highlights the challenges of forecasting due to season-to-season variability and limited dynamical history. Using a data-driven approach, the study generated weekly forecasts for the 2024-2025 seasons and submitted them to the CDC's FluSight Forecast Hub and the University of Guelph's AI4CastingHub. The results show that Hankel-DMD provides high-quality forecasts at the start and end of the season but overestimates the peak during the middle, leading to worse than baseline performance. The study suggests that while Hankel-DMD has potential as an efficient and interpretable forecasting method, its performance during the peak of the season requires further improvement. The findings are significant for public health planning but are limited by the retrospective nature of the analysis and the small number of models used for comparison. The evidence is moderate, as the performance was evaluated across the entire season, and the method's effectiveness during the peak remains uncertain.

title: Dual-aptamer magnetic capture and electrochemical detection of influenza B and respiratory syncytial viruses in artificial saliva.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the challenge of detecting respiratory viruses in saliva, which is a non-invasive specimen but difficult to work with due to its biochemical complexity. The research sought to develop a method that could overcome these challenges for accurate virus detection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the development and testing of a dual-aptamer magnetic-capture electrochemical assay for detecting influenza B virus (IBV) and human respiratory syncytial virus (hRSV) in artificial saliva. The method was designed to be applicable to emerging respiratory pathogens through aptamer substitution.
analysis.methods: The method utilized two sequence-distinct DNA aptamers for each target virus: a capture aptamer covalently attached to magnetic microparticles and a detection aptamer self-assembled on gold electrodes. The assay involved a single multiplexed batch capture step followed by parallel analysis on the two aptamer-modified electrodes using square-wave voltammetry.
analysis.main_results: Langmuir analysis of the square-wave voltammetry calibration curves yielded apparent dissociation constants of Kd = 177 ± 62 PFU mL-1 for IBV and 226 ± 85 PFU mL-1 for hRSV, with detection limits of 15 and 11 PFU mL-1, respectively. The log-linear calibration spanned 101-104 PFU mL-1 on both channels with sensitivities of 8.58 and 6.61 μA per decade.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the results as demonstrating the effectiveness of the dual-aptamer approach in detecting both IBV and hRSV in artificial saliva. The novelty lies in the proposed structural mitigation using sequence-orthogonal dual-aptamer geometry for capture and detection.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide a promising method for the non-invasive detection of respiratory viruses in saliva, which could enhance surveillance and diagnosis capabilities for respiratory syncytial virus and other emerging pathogens.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is a proof-of-concept and does not report on clinical validation or real-world application. The evidence is based on artificial saliva and may not fully represent the complexity of human samples, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents a dual-aptamer magnetic capture and electrochemical detection method for identifying influenza B virus (IBV) and human respiratory syncytial virus (hRSV) in artificial saliva. The approach uses sequence-distinct DNA aptamers for capture and detection, targeting non-identical epitopes. The method demonstrated apparent dissociation constants of Kd = 177 ± 62 PFU mL-1 for IBV and 226 ± 85 PFU mL-1 for hRSV, with detection limits of 15 and 11 PFU mL-1, respectively. The log-linear calibration spanned 101-104 PFU mL-1 with high sensitivity. The authors propose this as a structural mitigation strategy for virus detection, highlighting its potential for reconfiguration to detect emerging respiratory pathogens. The study is a proof-of-concept and does not include clinical validation, which limits its generalizability and results in a moderate confidence assessment.

title: Actin remodeling by human RNA virus: mechanisms and targeted intervention

analysis.scope_and_question: The article examines the molecular mechanisms by which human RNA viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), hijack the host actin network to influence viral replication and transmission efficiency. It focuses on the role of actin remodeling as a core host mechanism exploited by RNA viruses, with an emphasis on RSV and its impact on disease progression.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is based on a comprehensive analysis of the actin cytoskeleton's role in RNA viral infection, including the mechanisms by which six representative human RNA viruses, including RSV, manipulate host actin dynamics. The review highlights the importance of actin in viral infection and summarizes recent advances in understanding these interactions.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Actin remodeling is a critical host mechanism that RNA viruses, including RSV, exploit to enhance their replication and transmission efficiency. The review identifies key regulatory molecules involved in actin dynamics and outlines the pathways by which RSV and other viruses manipulate the host actin network.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review acknowledges that while actin remodeling is well-established as a host mechanism for RNA viruses, the clinical application of targeting actin signaling pathways remains challenging due to difficulties in balancing cytotoxicity and efficacy. There is also a need for further research on antiviral compounds that specifically target actin-related pathways in RSV.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review emphasizes the potential of targeting host factors like actin signaling pathways for broad-spectrum antiviral strategies. It suggests that future research should focus on developing antiviral compounds that effectively modulate actin dynamics without causing significant cytotoxicity, particularly for RSV.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the molecular mechanisms by which respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and other human RNA viruses manipulate the host actin network to enhance replication and transmission. It highlights the central role of actin remodeling in viral infection and identifies key regulatory molecules involved in this process. The article also discusses the potential of targeting actin signaling pathways for antiviral interventions, while noting the challenges in balancing efficacy and cytotoxicity. Future research is recommended to develop specific antiviral compounds that modulate actin dynamics without harmful side effects, offering a promising strategy for combating RSV and other RNA viruses.

title: Size, cytopathic effects, and prevalence of Influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and RSV in healthcare settings

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess airborne transmission of respiratory viruses in healthcare settings, focusing on the size and viability of virus-containing aerosols, particularly for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study collected size-resolved airborne samples in a dental clinic and hospital during the 2024-2025 respiratory virus season, with 81 sampling events conducted across different locations.
analysis.methods: Airborne samples were collected using a BC-BioSpot VIVAS (Viable Virus Aerosol Sampler) and analyzed by RT-PCR and culture-based assays for influenza A, influenza B, SARS-CoV-2, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
analysis.main_results: Viral RNA was detected in 11.1% of the 81 sampling events, with the highest positivity (25%) observed in pulmonary unit patient rooms. All RSV RNA was detected in the <1.5 μm size fraction.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight virus-specific differences in aerosol size distributions and the challenges of recovering viable virus from field-collected bioaerosols in healthcare environments.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform the development of targeted surveillance and control strategies for RSV in healthcare settings, particularly regarding aerosol size and viability.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to abstract-only evidence, and the results are based on molecular detection rather than direct infectiousness assessment, which may affect the strength of the conclusions.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated airborne transmission of respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), in healthcare settings during the 2024-2025 season. Using a BC-BioSpot VIVAS sampler, size-resolved airborne samples were collected in a dental clinic and hospital. RT-PCR and culture-based assays identified viral RNA in 11.1% of sampling events, with RSV RNA predominantly detected in the <1.5 μm size fraction. The results emphasize virus-specific differences in aerosol size distributions and the challenges of recovering viable RSV from field samples. While the findings contribute to understanding RSV transmission dynamics, the study relies on molecular detection rather than direct infectiousness assessment, limiting the strength of the evidence. These results may inform targeted surveillance and control strategies for RSV in healthcare environments.

title: IL-33 signaling uncouples pulmonary regulatory T-cell specialization from suppressive function during type 2 inflammation

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how regulatory T (TREG) cells fail to restrain exaggerated type 2 immune responses, particularly in the context of neonatal respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, which is strongly associated with asthma susceptibility later in life despite the persistent presence of pulmonary TREG cells.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used complementary murine neonatal RSV infection and allergic airway inflammation models to investigate the role of IL-33–IL-4Rα signaling in reprogramming pulmonary TREG-cell function.
analysis.methods: The researchers employed murine models of neonatal RSV infection and allergic airway inflammation to identify the IL-33–IL-4Rα signaling axis and its effects on pulmonary TREG-cell function.
analysis.main_results: IL-33 increased IL-4Rα expression, enhancing glycolysis-dependent STAT6 signaling and promoting GATA3-dependent functional specialization of pulmonary TREG cells.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings reveal that IL-33 acts as a developmental checkpoint that coordinately programs pathogenic TH2 memory and dysfunctional pulmonary TREG cell responses following exaggerated type 2 immune responses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide insights into the mechanisms underlying the failure of TREG cells to suppress type 2 inflammation, which could inform future strategies for asthma prevention and treatment.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on murine models, which may not fully translate to human conditions, and the evidence is derived from abstract-only data, limiting the confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates how IL-33 signaling affects the function of regulatory T (TREG) cells during type 2 inflammation, particularly in the context of neonatal respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. The research uses murine models to identify an IL-33–IL-4Rα signaling axis that reprograms pulmonary TREG-cell function. The results show that IL-33 enhances glycolysis-dependent STAT6 signaling and promotes GATA3-dependent functional specialization of TREG cells. analysis.scope_and_question: Clinical trials and observational studies demonstrate that both adjuvanted (RSVPreF3/AS01E) and non-adjuvanted (bivalent RSVpreF) vaccines provide substantial and comparable protection against RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease and hospitalization with comparable safety.

analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Overall, these findings suggest that effective protection against RSV disease in adults can be achieved with or without adjuvantation.

analysis.summary_en: Clinical trials and observational studies demonstrate that both adjuvanted (RSVPreF3/AS01E) and non-adjuvanted (bivalent RSVpreF) vaccines provide substantial and comparable protection against RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease and hospitalization with comparable safety. This narrative review examines the role of adjuvants in RSV vaccine development, with a focus on immunogenicity, vaccine effectiveness, safety, and implications for older adults and immunocompromised (IC) populations. Overall, these findings suggest that effective protection against RSV disease in adults can be achieved with or without adjuvantation. The totality of evidence to date does not suggest an effectiveness advantage for adjuvanted vaccines among IC populations. Among licensed protein subunit vaccines, key design differences include the use of adjuvants and antigen valency, raising important questions regarding the necessity and impact of adjuvantation for RSV prevention.

title: TRIM69 Suppresses the Cellular AMPK Pathway to Inhibit Viral Replication

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the role of TRIM69 in antiviral defense by targeting cellular pathways required for viral infection, addressing the need to understand how ISGs contribute to host innate immune responses against viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the use of ectopic expression of TRIM69 and knockdown of endogenous TRIM69 in cell lines to examine the effects on viral replication and cellular signaling pathways.
analysis.methods: TRIM69 was ectopically expressed and endogenous TRIM69 was knocked down to assess its impact on viral replication and cellular AMPK signaling. Assays included monitoring of autophagy, AMPK phosphorylation, and viral replication in response to viral infection and nutrient deprivation.
analysis.main_results: TRIM69 inhibited Sendai virus-induced autophagy and suppressed AMPK phosphorylation and its downstream target ULK1. TRIM69 strongly restricted replication of paramyxoviruses, pneumoviruses, and herpesviruses, including Sendai virus, respiratory syncytial virus, human parainfluenza virus type 3, and herpes simplex virus type 1.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that TRIM69 targets the cellular AMPK pathway to restrict viral replication, providing a novel mechanism for ISG-mediated antiviral defense.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: TRIM69 supports the expression of antiviral genes and amplifies innate antiviral signaling, which could inform the development of therapeutic strategies to enhance host innate immune responses against viruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of cell lines and the absence of in vivo models, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. The evidence strength is moderate due to the lack of randomized controlled trials and animal models.

analysis.summary_en: This study demonstrated that TRIM69, an interferon- and virus-inducible antiviral factor, targets the cellular AMPK pathway to restrict viral replication. TRIM69 also supports the expression of antiviral genes, suggesting a novel mechanism for ISG-mediated antiviral defense.

title: Is Wastewater Surveillance Predictive during the Endemic Phase of Respiratory Disease? An Analysis Based on Clinical, Wastewater, and Digital Search Data in Detroit, Michigan

analysis.research_question_and_background: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) has emerged as a major public health innovation catalyzed by the COVID-19 pandemic. However, its potential remains underexplored during and after COVID-19’s transition to endemicity.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study evaluates WBE’s potential to identify the pandemic-to-endemic transition of SARS-CoV-2 and to provide early warnings across multiple surveillance systems for influenza A (IAV) and B (IBV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 in the postpandemic era. We monitored SARS-CoV-2 N1 concentrations in wastewater from April 8, 2020, and July 31, 2025, generating the earliest and longest-running wastewater dataset in Detroit, MI.
analysis.methods: Pearson correlations were implemented to quantify the associations between wastewater concentrations and clinical, syndromic, and digital epidemiological data. Time-lagged cross-correlation (TLCC) was used to examine temporal dynamics among these datasets and identify the earliest emerging data for each disease and time lags. Extensive literature studies were conducted to elucidate the time-lag mechanisms for each disease, embracing the TLCC results.
analysis.main_results: During the endemic phase, from October 1, 2022, and March 31, 2025, we monitored RSV, IAV, IBV, and SARS-CoV-2 in Detroit’s wastewater.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: This study demonstrates the predictive value of WBE during the endemic phase, providing early warnings and predictions for seasonal respiratory diseases, including COVID-19, influenza, and flu-like disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: This study systematically analyzes the relationships of wastewater data to traditional clinical, syndromic, and digital epidemiological surveillance data during the endemic phase of these respiratory diseases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report specific limitations of the study design or evidence strength assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the predictive value of wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) during the endemic phase of respiratory diseases, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza A (IAV), influenza B (IBV), and SARS-CoV-2. The research evaluates WBE's potential to identify the pandemic-to-endemic transition of SARS-CoV-2 and provide early warnings for seasonal respiratory diseases. Wastewater data from Detroit, MI, were monitored from April 2020 to July 2025, with a focus on SARS-CoV-2 N1 concentrations. Pearson correlations and time-lagged cross-correlation (TLCC) were used to analyze associations between wastewater data and clinical, syndromic, and digital epidemiological data. The study demonstrates that WBE can offer early warnings and predictions for respiratory diseases during the endemic phase. However, the evidence does not report specific limitations or an assessment of the study's evidence strength.

title: Respiratory pathogen profiles in children aged 0–18 years: a single-center experience (October 2024 – June 2025)

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the clinical challenge of distinguishing active pediatric respiratory infections from upper respiratory tract colonization and interpreting etiology from routine host laboratory markers.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective surveillance of 784 PCR-positive pediatric cases (aged 0–18 years) was conducted between October 2024 and June 2025.
analysis.methods: Multiplex PCR was used to evaluate pathogen profiles, temporal dynamics, codetection patterns, and associations with C-reactive protein (CRP), albumin, absolute neutrophil count (ANC), and absolute lymphocyte count (ALC).
analysis.main_results: Viruses predominated (60.5%), with rhinovirus/enterovirus (32.1%), influenza viruses (26.1%), RSV (16.6%), and adenovirus (14.8%) being the most common. pneumoniae (38.9%) and H. influenzae (31.6%) were also detected. Influenza detections were associated with significantly lower median ANC ( p < 0.001), while adenovirus showed elevated CRP and ANC ( p < 0.001). pneumoniae exhibited elevated CRP and relative lymphopenia ( p < 0.001).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found distinct observational associations of routine host biomarkers across viral and bacterial PCR detection groups, highlighting the need for cautious interpretation of commensal bacteria alongside systemic inflammatory markers.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for pediatric respiratory infections, particularly in distinguishing active infections from colonization.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and the potential for bias in PCR detection. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the detection spectrum of pediatric respiratory pathogens and found that viruses predominated, with distinct associations of routine host biomarkers across viral and bacterial PCR detection groups. The findings can inform surveillance and diagnosis of pediatric respiratory infections.

title: From Concept to Clinical Trial: Starting Clinical Trials with a New Vaccine

analysis.research_question_and_background: Abstract Vaccine development is complex, and there are many things that need to be taken into consideration at every step.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The Investigator Brochure (IB) informs investigators and site staff about clinical aspects of the study vaccine.
analysis.methods: The vaccine needs to address an unmet medical need that can be measured in a pivotal phase 3 study.
analysis.main_results: There are many options for the design of a first-in-human (FIH) phase 1 vaccine clinical trial to be covered in the Clinical Trial Protocol (CTP).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Once the protocol is final, Informed Consent Documents (ICD), site management plans and other study-related documents must be prepared.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Regulatory and ethics committee applications must be submitted and approved, and clinical trial sites prepared.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The FIH study provides medical and financial justification for progressing into larger clinical trials, so it is usually performed under pressure to deliver rapid results but also must meet rigorous ethical, safety and quality standards.

analysis.summary_en: Abstract Vaccine development is complex, and there are many things that need to be taken into consideration at every step. The Investigator Brochure (IB) informs investigators and site staff about clinical aspects of the study vaccine. The vaccine needs to address an unmet medical need that can be measured in a pivotal phase 3 study. There are many options for the design of a first-in-human (FIH) phase 1 vaccine clinical trial to be covered in the Clinical Trial Protocol (CTP). Once the protocol is final, Informed Consent Documents (ICD), site management plans and other study-related documents must be prepared. Regulatory and ethics committee applications must be submitted and approved, and clinical trial sites prepared. The FIH study provides medical and financial justification for progressing into larger clinical trials, so it is usually performed under pressure to deliver rapid results but also must meet rigorous ethical, safety and quality standards.
